what_it_does: AI accelerator chips (like Google's TPU family) waste 30–72% of their active energy on 'leakage power' — electricity that bleeds away even when a circuit is sitting idle — because they have no way to switch off unused parts mid-computation. This paper introduces ReGate, a hardware-software system that selectively powers down idle components on these chips while they run real AI workloads, cutting total energy use by up to 32.8% with less than 0.5% slowdown.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Every chip has transistors that leak current even when not computing. In CPUs and GPUs this is managed by detecting idle periods and cutting power — a technique called power gating. But AI accelerator chips have a very different design: a large grid of multiply-accumulate units (called a systolic array, essentially a matrix of tiny multipliers that pass results to their neighbors), a software-managed fast scratchpad memory (on-chip SRAM — fast storage on the chip itself), and a rigid, pre-scheduled instruction pipeline. Standard CPU/GPU tricks don't transfer directly.

How it works — three strategies for three component types:

For the systolic array (the main computing grid). The grid is spatially underused when matrices are small. ReGate watches which rows and columns of the grid carry any non-zero weights. A small prefix-sum circuit (a chain of OR gates) figures out which rows/columns can be fully powered off and which need to stay on. For the case where only a few rows of input data are active, power-on signals follow the natural diagonal path that data already takes through the grid — so adjacent units wake each other up just in time, hiding almost all the wake-up delay.

For inter-chip links and the memory controller. These are only active during cross-chip communication bursts (called collective operations, e.g., summing partial results across chips). Between those bursts they sit idle for microseconds — long enough for a simple idle-detection circuit to cut their power and restore it before the next burst.

For vector units and SRAM scratchpad. These have unpredictable idle patterns that depend on the workload. Instead of guessing in hardware, the paper extends the chip's instruction set with a new 'setpm' instruction (set power mode). The compiler — which already knows the exact schedule of every instruction — inserts setpm on/off commands at precisely the right moments, with no runtime guessing.

The result. Tested on a production-level TPU simulator across LLM training, LLM inference, recommendation models, and image generation workloads, ReGate saves 8.5–32.8% energy (15.5% on average) and adds only 3.3% chip area. At data-center scale, this translates to a 31–63% reduction in operational carbon emissions.
